overview: The file documents U.S. State Department deliberations during 1949 over whether occupation policy should be revised to permit civil aviation in Japan. Its principal memorandum reviews existing prohibitions, competing proposals within the Far Eastern Commission, possible Japanese participation, security concerns, the economic case for domestic air service, and whether the Air Coordinating Committee should formulate a new U.S. position. A later memorandum questions whether pursuing agreement in the Commission remains worthwhile with a Japanese peace conference and treaty approaching, while the final document records Scandinavian Airlines' inquiry about extending its Hong Kong service to Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on civil aviation policy for Japan
subfiles.from: TRC – Mr. Barringer; identified elsewhere as prepared by Mr. Wolf of AV
subfiles.to: FE – Mr. Allison, through NA – Mr. Moseley, OFD – Mr. Barnett, and FE – Mr. Amrine
subfiles.about: The memorandum considers how the United States might obtain Far Eastern Commission support for allowing SCAP to authorize civil air services needed by occupied Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reviews post-surrender restrictions on Japanese aviation and summarizes U.S., Commonwealth, Chinese, Dutch, Soviet, French, Philippine, and New Zealand positions in the Far Eastern Commission. It argues that further Commission negotiations should await a clearer determination of Japan's need for domestic air service and the permissible extent of Japanese control or participation. Proposed benefits include faster mail and cargo movement, business and tourist travel, improved access to production areas, and support for foreign trade. It recommends confidential consultation with Commonwealth governments, referral of the issue to the Air Coordinating Committee, and a later State Department decision on whether to proceed through the Far Eastern Commission or another channel.

subfiles.title: Moseley memorandum to Merchant on civil aviation policy
subfiles.about: Moseley asks Merchant to advise whether the Department should continue seeking a Far Eastern Commission policy on civil aviation in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Moseley describes Japanese civil aviation as a longstanding issue for which field support and evidence of need remain weak. Although State Department officials had generally favored obtaining Commonwealth views and referring the problem to the Air Coordinating Committee, the prospect of a Japanese peace conference and treaty makes a difficult Far Eastern Commission campaign less attractive. He notes Commonwealth resistance to granting Japan greater responsibility and suggests consulting Hamilton, Amrine, and possibly Sebald before proceeding.

subfiles.title: Telephone conversation with Scandinavian Airlines about Tokyo service
subfiles.to: Department of State files; copies to Mr. Carter and Mr. Moseley
subfiles.about: The memorandum records Scandinavian Airlines' inquiry about applying to extend its Hong Kong service to Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Mr. Hale asked how Scandinavian Airlines should seek occupation approval for a proposed Hong Kong–Tokyo extension. Amrine advised that because Norway, Sweden, and Denmark were not occupying powers, the company should probably apply directly to SCAP and contact John Sherman, the official responsible for aviation matters in occupied areas.

interest: The file is useful for tracing the transition from punitive postwar restrictions on Japanese aviation toward consideration of its economic and administrative value during the occupation. The detailed comparison of national positions in the Far Eastern Commission exposes disagreements over Japanese participation, international control, security screening, technical standards, and domestic cabotage. The later documents show how the approaching peace settlement reduced enthusiasm for negotiating a new occupation directive even as foreign airlines were already seeking practical access to Tokyo.
